name: Vyākaraṇa (the grammarian-philosophers; śabdādvaita)
alt_names: the school of the three sages (munitraya)

tradition.text: grammar is an eternal limb of the Veda; the phonemes were revealed by Śiva's drum to Pāṇini (Nandikeśvarakāśikā 1; Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 56–57)

scholarly.text: Pāṇini c. 4th c. BCE; Patañjali c. 150 BCE; Bhartṛhari c. 5th c. CE; Nāgeśa d. c. 1755 CE

transmissions_received.what: speech (vāc) as a cosmic power with four quarters, three hidden (RV 1.164.45; RV 10.125; RV 4.58.3 read as praise of grammar)
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahābhāṣya Paspaśā reads RV 4.58.3 and 1.164.45 as praises of grammar (tea:mahabhasya:paspasa/4)

transmissions_received.what: Oṃ as the sound-form of Brahman and the two brahmans (śabda and para) (Maitrī 6.22)
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhartṛhari's Vṛtti cites Upaniṣadic passages on the word-brahman (reference from memory)

transmissions_received.what: the technical grammar of Pāṇini, Kātyāyana and Patañjali on which the philosophy is built
transmissions_received.evidence: VP 2 closing verses on the transmission of the Mahābhāṣya

transmissions_given.what: the levels of speech (vaikharī, madhyamā, paśyantī), pratibhā, and speech as reflexive awareness (pratyavamarśa), reworked with parā vāk above paśyantī
the name and model of dhvani (suggestion) — Ānandavardhana credits the grammarians' sphoṭa/dhvani doctrine; pratibhā
śabda-brahman, the levels of speech located in the body, and the theory of the letters (mātṛkā)
Maṇḍana Miśra's defence of sphoṭa and his sympathetic treatment of the word-brahman
Dignāga's engagement with Bhartṛhari on word-meaning and time (scholarly hypothesis)

distinctive_positions: Brahman, without beginning or end, is the principle of the Word (śabdatattva), the imperishable, which appears (vivartate) as things; from it the world proceeds (VP 1.1).
The one Brahman appears as many through its powers, of which time (kāla-śakti) is the chief (VP 1.2–3).
There is no cognition in the world not interpenetrated by the word; all knowledge shines as if pierced by the word (VP 1.123 Iyer).

The meaning-bearer is the sphoṭa, a partless, sequence-less word manifested by the sequential sounds (dhvani/nāda); the sentence (vākya-sphoṭa) is the real unit and word-meanings are abstractions from it (apoddhāra).
The meaning of a sentence is grasped as a flash of intuition (pratibhā), which even guides animals' instinctive action (VP 2.143–152).
Speech has three levels — vaikharī (articulated), madhyamā (mental, sequential), paśyantī (undivided, 'seeing'); the highest is the Veda's supreme station (VP 1.142 Iyer).
Grammar is the door to liberation, the remedy for the impurities of speech, the straight royal road to the highest (VP 1.14–16); the purified use of words is a yoga of the word (śabdapūrva-yoga).
Word, meaning and their relation are eternal (siddhe śabdārthasambandhe — Kātyāyana's first vārttika); grammar only restricts correct usage for the sake of merit (dharma-niyama).
Reasoning without scripture is unstable: what is inferred with effort by the skilled is explained otherwise by the more skilled (VP 1.34).
Every word ultimately denotes Being (sattā), the great universal, which is Brahman (VP 3.1, 3.2).
summary: The Pāṇinian grammarians as a school of philosophy of language. From Patañjali's question 'what is the word?' and Kātyāyana's doctrine of the eternal word, Bhartṛhari's Vākyapadīya built a monism of the Word: Brahman is the Word-principle that appears as the world, all cognition is word-permeated, meaning is borne by the indivisible sphoṭa and grasped as pratibhā, and grammar itself is a path to liberation. Maṇḍana Miśra defended sphoṭa; Helārāja, Puṇyarāja and Kaiyaṭa commented; Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita, Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa and Nāgeśa systematized the 'new' grammatical philosophy. Opposed by Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, Buddhists, Jains and (on paśyantī) the Kashmir Śaivas.

name: Alaṅkāraśāstra and Nāṭyaśāstra (poetics, dramaturgy and the theory of rasa)

tradition.text: drama (nāṭya) was made by Brahmā as a fifth Veda at the gods' request and taught to Bharata (NŚ 1.11–17)

scholarly.text: Nāṭyaśāstra compiled c. 200 BCE–400 CE; Bhāmaha and Daṇḍin c. 7th c.; Ānandavardhana c. 850; Abhinavagupta c. 975–1025; Jagannātha 17th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Nāṭyaveda drawn from the four Vedas: recitation from the Ṛg, song from the Sāman, gesture from the Yajus, rasas from the Atharva (NŚ 1.17)
the term and model of dhvani, and pratibhā
transmissions_received.evidence: Dhvanyāloka 1.13 vṛtti credits the grammarians (reference from memory)

transmissions_received.what: Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's 'bhāvanā' (bhāvakatva) modelled on Mīmāṃsā's word-power of bringing-about
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly reading of the reports in the Abhinavabhāratī

transmissions_received.what: Śaṅkuka's theory of rasa as inference
Abhinavagupta's reading of rasa as relish of consciousness itself (camatkāra, viśrānti)

transmissions_given.what: the rasa apparatus (sthāyibhāva, vibhāva, anubhāva, vyabhicārin, sāttvika) turned into bhakti-rasa by Rūpa Gosvāmī
rasa as the aim of music and the assignment of notes and rāgas to rasas (ŚR; Nāṭyaśāstra 29)
Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Bhaktirasāyana treating devotion as a rasa

distinctive_positions: Drama is a fifth Veda made for all classes, since the Vedas may not be heard by śūdras (NŚ 1.12); it imitates the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.107) and gives rest to the afflicted (NŚ 1.114).
Rasa arises from the union of determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva) and transient states (vyabhicāribhāva) (the rasa-sūtra, NŚ 6).
There are eight rasas in drama (NŚ 6.15); many later authorities add śānta as the ninth, with dispassion, calm or knowledge of reality as its stable emotion.
Rasa is relished (āsvādyate) as food flavoured by many ingredients is tasted by the discerning (NŚ 6.31–33).
Suggestion (dhvani) is the soul of poetry (Dhvanyāloka 1.1), and rasa is known only by suggestion.
Aesthetic relish is 'the twin brother of tasting Brahman' (brahmāsvāda-sahodara, SD 3.2), free of contact with other objects — akin to, but not identical with, realization.
For Abhinavagupta, rasa is the relish of one's own consciousness freed from personal limitation through generalization (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa); it is blocked by seven obstacles (vighna).
Poetry yields fame, wealth, knowledge of conduct, removal of evil, immediate supreme bliss and counsel like that of a beloved (KP 1.2).
summary: The science of drama and poetry from Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra to Jagannātha. Its central doctrine is rasa: the relish of an emotion, universalized through the art-work, in the heart of the sensitive spectator (sahṛdaya). The debate on how rasa arises (Lollaṭa, Śaṅkuka, Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka, Abhinavagupta), Ānandavardhana's theory of suggestion, and the recognition of śānta ('peace') as a rasa akin to liberation made poetics a theory of aesthetic experience that later fed devotional theology (bhakti-rasa).

name: Saṅgītaśāstra (the science of music: song, instrument and dance)
regions: all India; the northern (Hindustānī) and southern (Karṇāṭaka) traditions diverge after c. 13th–16th c.

tradition.text: music (gāndharva) descends from Brahmā and Śiva, taught by Nārada, Tumburu and Bharata; its mārga form was 'sought out' by Brahmā and others (ŚR 1.1.22)

scholarly.text: Nāradīya Śikṣā and Dattila c. early centuries CE (uncertain); Bṛhaddeśī c. 6th–9th c.; Saṅgītaratnākara c. 1210–1247; Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā c. 1620

transmissions_received.what: the seven notes of Sāman chant mapped to the flute's notes (Nāradīya Śikṣā 1.5.1–2)
rasa as the goal of performance; the Nāṭyaśāstra's music chapters (28–33)
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚR chapter 7 on nartana and rasa

transmissions_received.what: the body's channels and centres as the seat of nāda (ŚR 1.2.120–144)
the verse 'caitanyaṃ sarvabhūtānām' and the nāda–bindu cosmogony (textual parallel with ŚT 1.13)

transmissions_given.what: the saṅgīta grammar of Karṇāṭaka music used for devotional song (Purandara Dāsa)

distinctive_positions: Song, instrumental music and dance together are called saṅgīta; it is twofold, mārga (divine, fixed, giving merit when performed before Śiva) and deśī (regional, pleasing the heart) (ŚR 1.1.21–23).
Song is made of nāda, instrument manifests nāda, dance follows both: everything depends on nāda; from nāda come letters, words, sentences, all dealings (ŚR 1.2.1–2; Bṛhaddeśī 16–17).
Nāda is twofold, struck (āhata) and unstruck (anāhata), and manifests in the body (piṇḍa) (ŚR 1.2.3).
Nāda-brahman is the consciousness of all beings unfolded as the world; by worshipping nāda one worships Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara (ŚR 1.3.1–2).
Sages worship the unstruck nāda by the guru's path, but because it lacks charm (rakti) the struck nāda is taught, which delights people and breaks worldly existence (ŚR 1.2.163–167).
Nāda is named from na (breath) and da (fire): it arises from their union (ŚR 1.3.6; Bṛhaddeśī 22).
Twenty-two śrutis arise from twenty-two channels attached to the upward channel at the heart; seven svaras arise from the śrutis (ŚR 1.3.8–25).
One who knows the vīṇā, the śrutis and tāla goes the way of liberation without effort (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.115).
summary: The classical science of music as recorded from the Nāradīya Śikṣā, Dattila and Mataṅga to Śārṅgadeva's Saṅgītaratnākara and the later rāga treatises. Beyond its technical content (śrutis, svaras, grāmas, mūrchanās, jātis, rāgas, tālas, instruments and dance), it teaches that the whole world depends on nāda, that nāda is Brahman, and that music is a path to both enjoyment and liberation — a view carried into practice by the singer-saints.

name: Mantraśāstra (the science of mantras: the smārta-tantric mantra manuals)
regions: Kashmir (as source of the Śaiva background)

tradition.text: mantras are eternal and revealed by Śiva, the Goddess or Viṣṇu; the manuals only collect them

scholarly.text: Prapañcasāra c. 10th–11th c. (uncertain); Śāradātilaka c. 11th–12th c.; Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary 1493/94; Mantramahodadhi 1589

transmissions_received.what: the Śaiva cosmogony of sound (Śiva–Śakti–nāda–bindu), mantra-initiation and nyāsa
Vaiṣṇava mantras and rites (Nārāyaṇa, Gopāla, Nṛsiṃha)
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚT and Mantramahodadhi chapters on Vaiṣṇava mantras

transmissions_received.what: Goddess mantras and the letters as the Goddess's body
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚT chapters on Tripurā, Tvaritā and others

transmissions_received.what: the name śabda-brahman and the levels of speech (the Padārthādarśa quotes grammarians)
Oṃ, the vyāhṛtis and the Gāyatrī
transmissions_received.evidence: ŚT chapter on the Gāyatrī (reference from memory)

transmissions_given.what: the Śāradātilaka and Prapañcasāra as authorities for temple and domestic tantra
the cosmogony of nāda and the verse 'caitanyaṃ sarvabhūtānām' (ŚR 1.3.1)

distinctive_positions: From the supreme Lord, being-consciousness-bliss, arose Śakti; from her nāda; from nāda bindu (ŚT 1.7); the supreme bindu divides into bindu, nāda and bīja — Śiva, Śakti and their union (ŚT 1.8–9).
From the dividing bindu arose unmanifest sound, called śabda-brahman; śabda-brahman is not the word or its meaning (both insentient) but the consciousness of all beings (ŚT 1.11–13).
Śabda-brahman dwells in the body of beings as kuṇḍalinī and manifests as the letters, in prose and verse (ŚT 1.14).
The fifty letters (mātṛkā) are the body of the Goddess and of every mantra; mantras are placed on the body (nyāsa).
Every mantra has a seer, metre and deity, a seed (bīja), power (śakti) and pin (kīlaka); mantras are male, female or neuter by their endings.
A mantra may be defective in some fifty ways (ŚT 2.64–70) and is purified by ten rites (ŚT 2.112–122); secrecy (gopana) is itself one of the ten.
Only a qualified guru may give a mantra, to a qualified disciple tested for one to four years (ŚT 2.141–153); a mantra is 'mastered' by puraścaraṇa before it is used.
Japa is spoken, whispered or mental, each far superior to the previous.
summary: The tradition of learned manuals that collect the mantras of many deities with their seers, metres, seeds, rules of initiation, purification, placement and repetition — above all the Śāradātilaka (with Rāghavabhaṭṭa's Padārthādarśa), the Prapañcasāra and the Mantramahodadhi. Their theory: the supreme becomes sound (nāda, bindu), sound becomes the fifty letters, the letters become mantras, and the mantra, given by a guru and repeated with its purifications, gives enjoyment and liberation.
